title: Views in ASP.NET Core
description: Learn about Razor views, layouts, partial views, view components, and how ASP.NET Core resolves and renders views.

data.text: ASP.NET Core Views are the UI layer of an MVC application. Each view is a `.cshtml` file that mixes standard HTML with Razor syntax — a lightweight markup that lets you write C# directly inside your markup. When a controller action returns a view, ASP.NET Core locates the matching `.cshtml` file, executes any Razor code inside it, and sends the resulting HTML to the browser.
Key View Concepts

terms.definition: A `.cshtml` file containing HTML and Razor markup that generates the response for a controller action.
A shared template (`_Layout.cshtml`) that wraps individual views with a consistent page structure.
A reusable `.cshtml` fragment that can be rendered inside another view.
A C# class that renders content server-side, similar to a mini-controller for view logic.
The `@` prefix used to switch from HTML to C# inside a `.cshtml` file.

data.text: How Views Are Located

When a controller calls `return View()`, ASP.NET Core searches for a matching `.cshtml` file in a predictable order. If it cannot find the file, you get a clear runtime error listing the locations it checked.

data.caption: How ASP.NET Core resolves a view file
data.definition:
flowchart TD
    A[Controller calls View()] --> B{Is view in Areas?}
    B -->|Yes| C[Search Areas/Name/Views/Controller/Action.cshtml]
    B -->|No| D[Search Views/Controller/Action.cshtml]
    C --> E{Found?}
    D --> E
    E -->|Yes| F[Render the view]
    E -->|No| G[Search Views/Shared/Action.cshtml]
    G --> H{Found?}
    H -->|Yes| F
    H -->|No| I[ViewNotFound error]

data.title: Convention over configuration
data.text: ASP.NET Core uses convention-based view lookup by default. Stick to the folder naming rules and you rarely need to specify a view path manually.
Creating a Simple View
A view file is created inside the `Views/<ControllerName>` folder (omit the `Controller` suffix). For a `HomeController` with an `About` action, create `Views/Home/About.cshtml`:

data.text: The `@` symbol switches from HTML to C#. Razor automatically HTML-encodes output for security — `@DateTime.Now` renders as text, not executable code.

data.title: Razor encoding
data.text: Razor HTML-encodes values by default. To render raw HTML, use `@Html.Raw(...)` — but only with trusted content.
Passing a Model to a View
Views are strongly typed. At the top of a `.cshtml` file, declare the model type with `@model`. The controller passes the model via `return View(model)`:

data.text: Layouts and Sections

A layout is a shared template stored in `Views/Shared/_Layout.cshtml`. It typically contains the HTML shell: `<head>`, navigation, footer, and a `@RenderBody()` placeholder where the child view's content appears.

data.title: Views/Shared/_Layout.cshtml — shared page template
data.content: A minimal layout using Bootstrap and RenderBody.
data.code:
MyApp
@RenderBody()
© 2024 - MyApp

data.text: The `_ViewStart.cshtml` file (placed in the `Views` folder) runs before every view. Its most common job is to set the default layout so you don't have to repeat it in every view:

data.title: Views/_ViewStart.cshtml
data.content: Sets the default layout for all views.

data.text: Layout Sections

Sections let a child view inject content into named placeholders inside the layout. Define a section in the child view with `@section Name { ... }` and render it in the layout with `@RenderSection("Name")`:

data.title: Defining and rendering layout sections
data.content: Child view defines sections; layout renders them.
data.code:
@section Scripts { }

@Model.Name

@Model.Description

@RenderSection("Scripts", required: false)

data.title: Required vs optional sections
data.text: Pass `required: false` (the second argument) to `@RenderSection()` when a section is not defined in every child view. Omitting it causes a runtime error if the section is missing.
Partial Views
A partial view is a `.cshtml` file designed to be embedded inside another view. It is ideal for repeating UI such as a product card, a comment thread, or a sidebar widget.

data.title: Rendering a partial view with a model
data.content: Use Html.PartialAsync or Html.RenderPartialAsync to embed a partial view.
data.code:
@model IEnumerable

All Products

@foreach (var product in Model) { @await Html.PartialAsync("_ProductCard", product) }

data.title: Views/Shared/_ProductCard.cshtml — the partial view
data.content: A reusable partial that renders a single product card.
data.code:
@model Product
@Model.Name

@Model.Price.ToString("C")

data.title: Views, Partial Views, and View Components

cards.title: View
cards.description: A full page rendered for a controller action.
cons: Not designed for reuse inside other views

cards.title: Partial View
cards.description: A reusable fragment of HTML embedded in another view.
cons: No server-side logic of its own

cards.title: View Component
cards.description: A C# class that renders content server-side with full DI support.
cons: More setup than a partial view

data.text: View Components

A view component is the right choice when you need server-side logic inside a reusable UI element. Unlike partial views, view components can use dependency injection, query a database, or call an API before rendering.
A view component consists of two parts: a C# class (deriving from `ViewComponent`) and a Razor view placed under `Views/Shared/Components/<ComponentName>/Default.cshtml`.

data.title: A simple Cart view component
data.content: View component class and its corresponding Razor view.

data.title: Views/Shared/Components/Cart/Default.cshtml
data.content: The Razor view rendered by the Cart view component.

data.text: Invoke the view component from any view or layout using `@await Component.InvokeAsync("Cart")`. The string `"Cart"` is the class name without the `ViewComponent` suffix.

data.title: Exercise: Build a product list with a shared layout and a partial view
data.description: Practice creating views, layouts, and partial views in a new ASP.NET Core MVC project.
steps: Create a new ASP.NET Core Web App (Model-View-Controller) project.
Add a `Product` model with `Name`, `Price`, and `InStock` properties.
Create a `ProductsController` with an `Index` action that passes a list of products to the view.
Loop through the products in `Index.cshtml` and render each using the partial.
Add an optional `Scripts` section in `Index.cshtml` and render it in the layout.
data.expectedOutcome: You will have a product listing page that uses a shared layout, a strongly-typed view, and a reusable partial view for each product card.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Views are `.cshtml` files that mix HTML with C# Razor syntax.
ASP.NET Core searches for views in the controller folder first, then Shared.
Layouts provide a consistent page structure via _Layout.cshtml and @RenderBody().
Sections let child views inject content into named layout placeholders.
Partial views are reusable fragments; view components add server-side logic.
@inject makes a registered service available directly inside a view.
data.takeaway: Views are the presentation layer. Mastering views, layouts, and partials is the foundation for everything else in this module — especially tag helpers, which transform the HTML that views produce.
